newsitem.title: UK: IRA fashions death from household items.
newsitem.headline: IRA fashions death from household items.

text.p: Tin cans, coffee jars and cooking gas cylinders. Inocuous items in any home. But in the hands of IRA armourers - lethal.
In remote farms and urban kitchens, shadowy experts of the Irish Republican Army's "engineering department" turn them into bombs and missiles to fight British rule of Norther Ireland.
Years of warfare on sprawling housing estates and rolling countryside have been fuelled not just by smuggled stocks of hi-tech foreign arms but with home-made bombs and missiles.
They have been fired with alarming intensity every couple of days this year at British army and local police patrols.
In the latest stage of a 28-year war that has killed more than 3,200, home-made grenades and rockets form part of the arsenal the IRA uses to drive Britain from the province.

Security officials say soldiers and police across the province are at high risk in the IRA's latest campaign which began when the guerrillas ended a 17-month truce one year ago with a headline-grabbing bomb at London's Canary Wharf complex.
"Alongside the commercially produced weaponry, they've always relied heavily on home-made type of weaponry. And they are just as effective," a senior security source told Reuters.
For "spectaculars" - the IRA term for a major attack - the guerrillas use Czech-made Semtex plastic explosive or massive amounts of ammonium nitrate-based fertiliser explosive .
Since relaunching its war one year ago, the IRA has set off massive bombs, packed into cars and lorries, in English cities, and at military headquarters in Northern Ireland.

Hidden in underground bunkers or sunk into sand dunes on lonely Irish beaches, like an arsenal uncovered on the north Donegal coast several years ago, the IRA is reckoned to have "enough rifles to arm a battalion" say security sources.
As well as around around 600 AK-47 assault rifles, around 20 heavy machine guns, and RPG-7 rocket launchers, it has around three tonnes of Semtex, officials believe.
For its relaunched hit-and-run street-corner war in Northern Ireland's towns and villages, the guerrillas opt mainly for smaller devices. Makeshift maybe, but they can kill, police say.

Slate-grey police vehicles, military camouflaged green armoured cars and heavily-defended security bases are targets for guerrillas firing from speeding cars or crouching in fields where they press a remote control button.
"Barrack-busters, PRIGS, and coffee jar bombs" are just some of the do-it-yourself weapons the guerrillas have perfected.
Tins that held beans or peas and jars that contained coffee or sweets are stuffed with powerful explosives and shrapnel.
Iron scaffolding is cut up into tubes and converted, with an array of firing mechanisms, into hand-held anti-tank style rocket launchers easily discarded by the fleeing attackers.
Industrial tubing is transformed into launch batteries to blast salvoes of squat gas-holders or torpedo-length rockets.

A PRIG "projected recoilless improvised grenade" usually has a kilo of high explosives packed into a tin can. Two packets of biscuits are also squeezed into the shoulder-held launch tube to cushion the "strike-back" recoil effect on the gunman.

The "coffee jar bomb" has half a kilo of explosive and nuts, bolts and padlocks. Lobbed over police station walls, it can be fatal. "Once it breaks, it detonates," said a police officer. Recently security forces found a variant, a two kilo "sweetie jar bomb", the first located in the renewed campaign, designed to be dropped from a height on a mobile patrol.
The commonly-used "Mark 12 horizontal mortar" is set by the roadside or dug into soft earth, its tail-finned anti-armour warhead detonated from a firing point some 100 yards away.

The "barrack buster" is an explosive-laden gas canister fired from the back of a lorry which , as its name implies, is designed to wreck security bases. It was used in more than 50 attacks before the 1994 ceasefire. Last June, the authorative Janes Intelligence Review, quoting British intelligence sources, reported that the IRA had developed a new high-powered "mark 17" mortar during its truce.
Last month, "An Phoblacht", the weekly organ of Sinn Fein, the IRA's political wing, reported that the guerrillas had used a new two-mortar weapon to attack police in County Down.

"The double mortar unit fired two missiles simultaneously at the RUC vehicle, skimming over it in front of a shocked driver," the paper said. "He narrowly missed death as the two exploded on contact with a high grass bank opposite the firing point...."

British security sources say they have had a string of successes in foiling attacks but they do not underestimate their foes. "At the moment there is no sign whatever of a ceasefire coming...," a detective said.
